catalog_citation: Lloyd, J.A. 1997. Contrastive and grammatically defined tone in Baruya. In Karl Franklin (ed.), Papers in Papuan Linguistics No. 2, 283-361. Pacific Linguistics A-85. Canberra: Australian National University. DOI 10.15144/PL-A85.283 (imprint line on p.283 reads 'Pacific Linguistics, A-85, 1996'; PL/sealang cover sheet gives 1997).
catalog_locator: p.283 sec. 1.1 Introduction; p.284 sec. 1.2.1; p.317 sec. 1.4 Conclusion and sec. 2.1-2.2 Stress and intonation.
catalog_quote: In the Baruya language there are three basic stem tone patterns contrasting low-low, high-low and low-high on the last two syllables of single-root stems (§1.2). Compound stems are very common. A root may have only one high tone, but a stem or word may have more than one. The additional high tones result from perturbation between roots, between stems and suffixes or between words in a phrase. High tones do not occur on contiguous syllables within a word, but may occur on alternate syllables. They can occur on contiguous syllables across word boundaries. After a low root, stem or word within a phrase, the first vowel of the following unit is perturbed to high. ... High-tone syllables are also stressed (stress equals loudness) without appreciably affecting the inherent length of the vowels ... Other syllables are low (unmarked) and unstressed. They tend to be slightly higher before or after a high syllable. There is a non-contrastive utterance initial stress and semi-high tone. High tones vary in pitch depending on their position in word, phrase, clause, sentence and utterance (§2). [p.283] ... One-syllable stems have low tone. ... Two- and three-syllable stems contrast high and low tones on the last two syllables. Most two-syllable stems are low. Very few are high-low. [p.284] ... High tone on words (§1) incorporates stress, but mid and high intonation are not stressed. [p.317]
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: No fixed stress position. Each root carries at most one lexical high tone ('pitch accent' in Lloyd 1969 and Lloyd & Healey 1970), located contrastively on the final or penultimate syllable of the stem, or none (all-low; most disyllabic stems are all-low). Stress (loudness) simply accompanies every high-toned syllable; low syllables are unstressed. Additional highs arise by sandhi: after an all-low root/stem/word the first vowel of the next unit becomes high; in noun compounds a dropped noun-marker syllable passes its tone to the next root; highs never fall on adjacent syllables within a word. The only tone-independent stress is a non-contrastive utterance-initial stress with semi-high pitch.
new_statements.secondary_stress: No word-level secondary stress described; a word may carry several high (=stressed) syllables on alternate syllables via perturbation. Above the word, phrase stress falls on the high tone of the central word of the phrase (or first word past centre), clause stress on the central phrase stress, sentence stress on the main stress of the second/final-verb clause (sec. 2.2, p.317-318).
new_statements.exceptions: One-syllable stems are low; very few two-syllable stems are high-low; four-syllable stems are all compounds subject to perturbation; transition vowel ɨ between roots is never perturbed to high; verbs: basic perturbation rule holds for future tenses and most negatives, three special rules for non-future tenses (sec. 1.3); example (5g) di'mudinya noted as an exception.
new_statements.domain_note: Statement is about roots/stems and phonological words, with perturbation operating across stem, suffix and word boundaries within the phrase; citation/utterance-final forms end in -o and carry final intonation on the last syllable (high/mid intonation not stressed). Lloyd 1969 p.32 gives the earlier formulation: 'There are three basic pitch accent patterns on noun stems. Most have no pitch accent, while others have pitch accent on either the ultimate or penultimate syllable.. The first syllable of the word, root or morpheme gains a pitch accent, unless the following syllable or either of the preceding two syllables has a basic pitch accent.'
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe the Baruya dialect proper (Wonenara/Marawaka, the largest tribe; the language also has Wantakia and Gulicha dialects, cf. Lloyd & Healey 1970 fn.). 1969-70 works spell it 'Barua'; later SIL materials also use 'Yipma'. Same languoid baru1267.

tone_statements.quote: Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length) Pitch-accent incorporates both high pitch and stress. Non-accented syllables are stressless with low pitch. Roots are accented on either the ultimate or penultimate syllable only. Therefore only three stem pitch patterns occur. Stress functions with tone. kwata 'frog sp.' tuta 'track' kwatá 'nut basher' tutá 'short' [...] Conventions: Orthographic Pitch-accent is not written.
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone_statements.summary: Culminative pitch accent (H = high pitch + stress) on root-final or root-penultimate syllable or absent -> three stem patterns (LL, HL, LH); unaccented syllables low; accent lexically contrastive (kwata vs kwatá); not written in orthography.
